To: Shared/Ops & HR
Replying to: none
Cc: none
Subject: DRAFT — Monday Embakasi casuals: pay update and response plan for Brian

Monday, 30 November | For Brian Ochieng
Draft for Achieng’s review before use

Brian,

This is a difficult conversation, but the first thing to remember is that the delay is our mistake, not the casuals’. They did nothing wrong. Go in ready to listen and take responsibility, not to defend the company or argue about whether people are entitled to be upset.

What happened with Friday’s pay

The bank rejected the bulk payment file on Friday because its new template rules were not met: the beneficiary reference field was too long. No payments in that file were processed. Finance did not see the rejection until after 5pm because the alert went to an old mailbox, by which time the bank cut-off had passed. This is why Friday’s pay did not arrive. It was a processing failure on our side, not an error by the casuals.

Management has approved an M-Pesa bulk payment instead. Kevin’s realistic timing is that money should reach phones on Monday by 11am. That is the time we can communicate; do not suggest it will arrive earlier or promise a precise minute. Peninah has confirmed 198 phone numbers. She could not reach 14 people, mostly new loaders from the Athi River intake. She will be at Embakasi from 7:30am with the list to verify those numbers face to face. The approved M-Pesa batch also includes KES 500 per affected casual for Monday lunch and fare. The company will cover the M-Pesa charges; nothing will be deducted from anyone’s payment.

What you can say

Be direct and apologise on management’s behalf. For example:

“I’m sorry. Your Friday pay did not come through because the payment file was rejected by the bank, and we did not catch that in time to meet the cut-off. That was our failure, not yours. Management has approved payment by M-Pesa, with the KES 500 lunch and fare support in the same batch. The current timing is by 11am today. We won’t tell you it will come earlier when we can’t guarantee that. Peninah is here from 7:30 to check details with anyone whose number needs correcting, and to help with payslips.”

If someone’s payment does not arrive, don’t dismiss the concern or guess at the cause. Ask Peninah to check the person’s details and payment status, note the person’s name and number, and tell them when and how you’ll update them. Don’t say a payment has landed until it has. Don’t suggest a person with an unconfirmed number has been paid.

What you must not promise or disclose

Do not promise payment before 11am, guarantee a particular arrival time, or say that every payment has already been sent. Do not promise anything beyond the approved lunch and fare support. Don’t speculate about why an individual payment may be missing; refer it to Peninah and Kevin to verify.

Keep the company’s cash position and internal financing arrangements out of this conversation and the document. If asked about them, bring the discussion back to the facts the team needs: Friday’s file was rejected, management has approved the M-Pesa route, and the current timing is by 11am. Do not invent a reason or share confidential internal information.

How to handle the Kisumu trucks

The Kisumu trucks need to leave by 9am to make the mill’s offloading slot. You’ll be at the depot from 5:30am, so use the time before the wider conversation to understand the situation. Joseph has reported that Ouma and two others are urging people not to load until they see the money. Don’t assume that is the whole group’s position, and don’t treat raising the concern as misconduct.

Speak with Ouma privately first, before addressing the whole group. Keep it calm and respectful. Ask what he and the others need answered, acknowledge that people may have rent due, and explain the confirmed pay information without overstating it. Ouma is upset, but that does not make him a bad person. Give him room to respond; don’t turn the private conversation into a confrontation or ask him to speak for everyone.

Then speak to the group, apologise, give the same clear update, and invite questions. Ask whether they are willing to load while the payment is being resolved, and listen to their answer. Be clear about the 9am departure and the mill slot, but don’t use that deadline to threaten people or imply they will lose their jobs if they refuse. Do not threaten contracts or dismissal. No one is to be dismissed or threatened with dismissal on the day.

If people refuse to load or a stoppage begins, do not try to break it up alone or handle it as a disciplinary matter. Pause and keep the conversation safe and orderly. Contact HR and manage the stoppage together with HR, as the procedure requires; do not treat a work stoppage as the grievance channel or resolve it through threats. Record the concerns and the key facts, including what was said about the trucks and what response was offered. Keep Joseph informed. Operations and HR should assess the immediate operational options together, including what can realistically be done about the 9am departure, without pressuring anyone or making up a new commitment. Route individual grievances through the shift supervisor and then HR within 48 hours.

Peninah will arrive at 7:30am with the list. Make sure the 14 people whose numbers could not be confirmed know where to find her, and give her space to verify their details privately. She can also print payslips for anyone who wants one.

Keep Achieng updated by WhatsApp before she boards if anything changes. She is up from 4:30am. In particular, let her know promptly if Kevin’s payment timing changes, if the number checks reveal a problem, or if the group’s decision puts the Kisumu departure at risk.

The aim is to be honest, accountable and calm: acknowledge the failure, give only the approved and supportable information, and handle any stoppage jointly with HR.
